raw_response:
Well, it's the start of the season and I need to sort out what to do with my 10 mu. I've only been back on the farm for two years — before that I was working construction in Shijiazhuang — so I'm still learning the ropes. Last year was rough. My eggplant got some kind of blight in July and I lost maybe a third of the crop because I thought I could save money by skipping the early fungicide sprays. Never again. The chili did okay though — prices at the village collection point were around 1.2 yuan per jin, so I'm keeping both vegetables. My wife and I do most of the work. Our son is in high school and can only help on weekends.

Here's how I'm thinking about each crop.

**Wheat:** I've got 4.5 mu of wheat in the ground from last October. Last spring I was too cheap with the topdressing — I only put down about 8 kg of urea per mu and the wheat turned yellow at jointing. Ended up with only about 800 jin per mu. This year I'm putting more, about 12 kg of urea per mu at green-up, and another 5 kg if it still looks pale. The extension guy said 10 kg total is enough, but I'd rather waste a little fertilizer than risk another bad wheat year. I'll irrigate three more times before harvest: now at green-up, once at jointing right after topdressing, and once at heading if April-May stays dry. One spray of herbicide in the field now, and I'll watch for powdery mildew.

**Summer maize:** After wheat harvest in mid-June, I'll plant maize right away on the same 4.5 mu — no-tillage, direct seeding into the stubble. That's what my neighbor Lao Wang does and it saves me almost a week, which I need for the vegetables. I'll buy hybrid seed, probably Nongda 372 or Denghai 605, about one package per mu at roughly 55 yuan. I'll put down compound fertilizer at sowing — about 80 jin per mu of the 28-6-6 blend. Two irrigations should be enough if the summer rains are normal.

**Eggplant:** This is my main cash crop — 3 mu. I'm buying seedlings from the seedling factory in town this year. Last year I tried growing my own in a small plastic tunnel and they got too leggy and weak. The market seedlings cost about 500 yuan per mu for around 2,200 plants, but at least they're strong and uniform. I'll transplant in early May when the soil has warmed up. Before planting I'll rotary till and make raised beds, then lay plastic mulch to keep moisture and control weeds — that's what the successful vegetable grower down the road does. Basal fertilizer: about 100 jin per mu of 15-15-15 compound, plus about 800 jin per mu of chicken manure I bought from the poultry farm. I'll topdress twice with special fertilizer — once when the first flowers set, and again in mid-summer during peak fruiting. Seven irrigations through the season. For pesticides, I'm starting early and regular this year because of last year's disaster: insecticide every 10 days or so, fungicide every two weeks starting right after transplanting, and one herbicide spray before laying mulch.

**Chili:** I've got 2.6 mu of chili. Also buying seedlings — about 2,800 plants per mu at around 350 yuan per mu. I'll plant a bit earlier than eggplant, in late April, since chili handles cool nights a little better. Basal fertilizer is about 80 jin per mu of 15-15-15 compound plus some chicken manure. One topdress at flowering with a high-potassium formula. Five irrigations. Same pesticide vigilance as eggplant — aphids and wilt are the main enemies. I need to stay on top of it.

**Labor and money:** The vegetables eat up labor. Just pruning and harvesting eggplant multiple times through summer is endless work. During peak season — June wheat harvest, maize planting, and first big eggplant harvests all at once — I'll have to hire day laborers. I'm budgeting about 10 hired days for eggplant and 5 for chili at 100-120 yuan per day. My wife and I will put in about 300+ family days across all crops.

Total input cost this year will run me about 10,000 yuan. That's basically all our savings from last year. It makes me nervous. If vegetable prices crash or disease hits again, we're in a hole. But the wheat and maize give us food security — we'll keep about 1,000 jin of wheat for our own flour — and the vegetables are where the cash income comes from. My neighbor says I should drop the grain and do all vegetables, but with only two years of experience I'm not ready to take that risk. Maybe in a couple more years.
